Batch pallet & fixture cleaning · wave soldering pallets, reflow coolers, SMT fixtures

Flux-caked pallets in. Production-ready fixtures out.
One basket. Three-stage filtration. No solvent, no scrubbing.

The SME-5200 is a fully automatic batch cleaning machine for wave soldering pallets, reflow oven coolers and SMT fixtures. Pallets load into a rotating SUS304 basket, take a 720-degree curtain of heated water-based cleaning liquid, rinse on warm tap water and leave dry under high-pressure hot air — while a closed-loop three-stage filter keeps the chemistry alive cycle after cycle. Water-based by design: flammable solvent is simply not an option on this machine.

01 — Why it matters

The pallet nobody cleans is the defect nobody traces

Wave soldering pallets, reflow coolers and selective-soldering fixtures spend their lives bathed in flux. The residue bakes on, cycle after cycle, until the fixture that is supposed to hold your board flat and mask your pads is itself the contamination source. Cleaning fixtures is not housekeeping — it is a yield step, and doing it by hand is the most expensive way to do it badly.

01

Baked-on flux defeats hand scrubbing

Flux that has been through two hundred solder cycles is not the flux you can wipe off a board. It is a hardened, partially carbonised film in the pockets, threads and spring channels of the fixture. A brush reaches the flat faces; the residue that matters lives where the brush cannot, and it transfers back onto the next board.

02

Solvent cleaning trades one risk for a worse one

Open-solvent soaking removes flux and adds fire load, VOC exposure, hazardous-waste manifests and an audit finding. The SME-5200 user manual is blunt about it: volatile organic cleaning solvents are strictly forbidden on this machine because they may cause fire or explosion. The safe chemistry is not a compromise — it is the design.

03

Fixtures waiting to be cleaned stop the line

A pallet queue is a hidden bottleneck: boards wait for a clean fixture, operators wait for a pallet, and the wave solder machine idles. A batch cleaner with a predictable cycle turns fixture cleaning from an interruption into a scheduled load — the same basket, the same recipe, the same result every time.

02 — The cycle

Six stages, one basket, zero solvent

The SME-5200 runs a closed batch cycle. Pallets are loaded into the rotating basket, the cover is locked, and the machine walks the load through wash, liquid recovery, rinse and hot-air dry while the filtration loop cleans the chemistry in parallel. Cycle times below are quoted from the 2020 user manual.

01

Load & lock · basket φ1000 mm

Pallets and fixtures stack into the round SUS304 basket up to 200 mm high (pallets to 450 mm cleaning height). The upper cover closes on air springs and locks; a guard switch stops the machine if the door is opened mid-cycle.

02

Wash · 5–15 min, 720° spray

The basket motor turns the load while upper, lower and front-side spray rods lay a heated water-based liquid curtain over it from every angle. Liquid is drawn from the 80 L tank through the filter barrel and heated to the set temperature — normally 40–45 °C, up to 80 °C for heavy soil.

03

Liquid recovery · 1 min

Compressed air blows the residual cleaning liquid out of the pipes, rods, nozzles and off the fixtures, back into the tank through the triple valve. This is the step that stretches chemistry life: the liquid you recover is liquid you do not buy.

04

Rinse · 1–2 min, warm tap water

A separate 80 L water tank and its own pump and pipework rinse the load on heated tap water — normally 40–45 °C. Keeping rinse water physically separate from cleaning liquid stops cross-contamination and protects bath strength.

05

Hot-air dry · 10–20 min

A high-pressure blower pushes air through an air heater to 80–90 °C (range room temperature to 90 °C) and air knives sheet the water off the load. Fixtures leave dry to the touch and go straight back to the line.

06

Filtration circuit · runs the whole cycle

In parallel with every stage, liquid recirculates through the three-stage filter: a 2 mm screen protects the pump, a 100 µm screen catches solder balls and solids, and five 20 µm cores pull the fine flux out. Clean liquid returns to the tank continuously.

Cycle times, tank capacities, temperatures and filtration grades are quoted from the SME-5200 user manual (2020) and the Southern Machinery filtration technical guide.

Why the build is stainless and the chemistry is water

SUS304 from tank to nozzle

Structure, piping and tanks are SUS304 stainless steel. Hot alkaline cleaning liquid and hot water never meet a painted or plastic part that can warp, corrode or leach into your bath.

Water-based by design, not by option

The machine is engineered for one chemistry: modern water-based cleaning agents. Flammable solvent is forbidden by the manual because it can cause fire or explosion — the hazard is designed out, not managed.

Rotating basket, 720° coverage

The basket motor turns the load while three liquid and three water spray rods cover it from above, below and the front side. Even spray pressure and offset nozzles mean no blind cleaning area, even in fixture pockets.

Three-stage recirculating filtration

A 2 mm screen guards the pump, a 100 µm screen stops solder balls and solids being re-sprayed onto fixtures, and five 20 µm cores return clean liquid to the tank. Chemistry life is measured in weeks, not cycles.

Separated liquid and water circuits

Dedicated 80 L tanks with independent pumps and pipework keep cleaning liquid and rinse water apart, so rinse water never dilutes the bath and the bath never contaminates the rinse.

Serviceable by one person

Filter elements swap in three moves — release pressure, undo six screws on the barrel, change the five cores. Spray rods, barrel and tanks are reachable without pulling the machine apart.

The control system protects the load, the chemistry and the operator

Recipes, not guesswork

Wash, rinse and dry times and the three temperatures are set on the touch panel and saved per fixture type and soil level, then recalled by name. The same pallet gets the same cycle on every shift.

Alarms that name the cause

Pressure alarms below 2.0 and above 7.0 kg/cm², heater over-temperature at +10 °C tolerance, tank level faults and a door guard switch all stop the cycle and say what tripped, on the panel.

Password-protected process

Soft parameter settings are password-protected so an operator cannot drift the validated cycle. What quality signed off is what the machine runs.

Proven components

Mitsubishi PLC and Schneider contactors — the parts your maintenance team already stocks and trusts — rather than orphan controllers with no spare path.

04 — Throughput

The batch maths, honestly

A batch cleaner is paced by its cycle, not by a conveyor: wash plus rinse plus dry, plus your load and unload time. The table gives baskets per 8-hour shift at the manual's published cycle times, ignoring load/unload so you can add your own handling allowance. Your real number also depends on how many fixtures fit in one basket — a φ1000 × 200 mm envelope holds far more small pallets than large ones.

Cycle = wash + rinse + dry, quoted from the 2020 manual (wash 5–15 min, rinse 1–2 min, dry 10–20 min). Figures exclude load and unload time; add your own handling allowance. One basket of small wave-solder pallets is many pallets — count fixtures per basket, not baskets per shift, when you size the line.

05 — Options

Configure the machine around your fixtures

The SME-5200 ships as a complete batch cleaner. These are the documented configuration points and standard extras worth deciding before you order — the first four are choices we make with you; the last two come with the machine.

Options quoted from documents

Cleaning height to your tallest fixture

Standard basket envelope is φ1000 × 200 mm with pallets to 450 mm; machines are built for other cleaning heights when your fixture stack demands it. Send the tallest fixture and we confirm the envelope.

Basket inserts and dividers

Inner basket arrangements and dividers keep small pallets, springs and hold-down pins separated so spray reaches every face and parts do not nest during rotation.

Chemistry matched to your soil

Water-based agents are selected for your flux type — rosin, no-clean or heavy baked-on residue — and validated in a trial on your own fixtures before you commit.

English operator interface

The machine ships with a Chinese touch interface as standard; an English operator interface is available for overseas lines and training.

Automatic liquid fill and drain

Standard: pneumatic diaphragm pumps fill and drain both tanks automatically, removing manual lifting, spilling and operator contact with hot chemistry.

Three-stage filtration with spare cores

Standard: 2 mm and 100 µm stainless screens plus five 20 µm cores, with a recommended spare core set so a filter change never waits for a shipment.

06 — Installation

What your floor needs before the crate arrives

The installation floor layout defines exactly what the machine expects. Plan these six items and commissioning is a formality; miss one and the machine waits. The footprint is compact — about 1.4 × 2.0 m — but the service clearances are not optional.

STEP 1

Site and clearance

Hard industrial floor with about 1.4 × 2.0 m of machine footprint. Reserve 1.5 m of clear access in front and 1 m at the side for maintenance, filter changes and liquid handling, per the official layout.

STEP 2

Power

AC 380 V, 50 Hz, 63 A supply with a properly rated isolator beside the machine. Total connected power about 33 kW across heaters, pumps, blower and basket motor.

STEP 3

Compressed air

0.5–0.7 MPa of dry clean air at 400–600 L/min. The air knives, the liquid-recovery blow-back and the diaphragm pumps all run on it continuously.

STEP 4

Water in

A tap-water connection for the 80 L rinse tank, filled and heated automatically. No DI plant is required for fixture rinsing — this machine rinses on warm tap water by design.

STEP 5

Drainage

Drain connections for spent cleaning liquid and rinse water at change-out. Keep the cleaning-liquid drain out of the general drain unless you have a waste-chemical collection point.

STEP 6

Exhaust and handling

One Φ120 mm vent ducted to outside extraction for air and vapour. The machine arrives at about 600 kg — move it on a lift platform or pallet truck, never by ropes.

ARTICLE 01The pallet nobody cleans is the defect nobody traces

Flux bakes onto wave soldering pallets cycle after cycle until the fixture holding your board is the contamination source. Here is the transfer path — and the three-place audit that finds it on your floor.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2020 user manual and the Southern Machinery technical documents.

Pull a wave soldering pallet out of the return queue and look at it under a good light. Not the top face — the pockets. The threads, the spring channels, the underside of the mask windows, the gap between the carrier and the hold-down pin. That is where the film lives: flux that spattered, flowed and baked, cycle after cycle, until it stopped being residue and became part of the fixture.

Here is the part nobody budgets for: that fixture now touches every board it holds. The baked film picks up solder balls and dust and transfers them onto clean pads; the mask window that should seal a joint now leaks solder because its sealing face is no longer flat. Your defect is not a soldering problem and not a board problem. It is a fixture problem wearing a soldering costume, and it will not show up in any soldering parameter you log.

So here is an audit you can run this week with nothing but a torch and a wipe. Three places, three questions. One: run a clean white wipe across the mask window sealing faces — what colour comes back? Two: look into the spring channels and threads with a torch — is there a hardened film or loose crumbly residue? Three: check the pallet return queue — how many pallets are waiting, and how long have the oldest ones waited? If the wipe is not white, the channels are caked, or the queue is older than a shift, you have a fixture cleanliness problem with a number on it.

Once you have the number, the fix is a cycle, not a bench. The SME-5200 loads the pallets into a rotating SUS304 basket, lays a heated water-based liquid curtain over them from above, below and the front side for five to fifteen minutes, recovers the chemistry with a compressed-air blow-back, rinses on warm tap water and dries on 80–90 °C hot air. The recipe is saved per fixture type. The same caked pallet gets the same cycle on every shift, and the three-stage filter keeps the bath clean while it works.

Keep the audit on the wall and run it monthly. The first audit finds the caked fixtures; the second finds the process change that re-caked them — a new flux, a hotter profile, a longer pallet loop. Factories that re-audit catch fixture degradation while it is still a wipe test, not a yield loss.

If you want the three-place audit done on your own pallets, send photos of your dirtiest fixtures to info@smthelp.com or on WhatsApp at +86 13602562576. We will run them through a trial cycle, photograph before and after, and tell you honestly whether your fixtures need a machine or just a better schedule.

ARTICLE 02Why solvent soaking is the most expensive way to clean a fixture

Open solvent removes flux and adds fire load, VOC exposure and hazardous waste. A cost and risk model in four lines, and the water-based route that removes both.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2020 user manual and the Southern Machinery technical documents.

Every factory that soaks fixtures in solvent eventually runs the same four-line cost model, and every one of them skips line three.

Line one is the solvent itself: drums purchased, decanted, topped up, and eventually hauled away as hazardous waste at a price per litre that surprises people. Line two is the people: someone lifts fixtures in and out of an open bath, in vapour, with gloves that are never quite the right gloves, for as long as you build the product. Line three is the one that gets skipped — the compliance stack: fire load in the insurance survey, VOC exposure in the ventilation assessment, hazardous-waste manifests, the audit finding that open solvent soaking next to a wave solder machine is exactly the kind of ignition pairing the surveyor writes up. Line four is the yield you never connect: solvent lifts flux but leaves it in the bath, and the tenth fixture out of a dirty bath comes out with a film of the first nine.

The alternative is not slower, it is engineered. The SME-5200 user manual is unambiguous: volatile organic cleaning solvents are strictly forbidden on this machine because they may cause fire or explosion. That sentence is the whole design philosophy. Water-based chemistry, heated to 40–45 °C normally and up to 80 °C for heavy soil, does the dissolving; rotation and a 720-degree spray curtain do the reaching; time does the rest.

What you lose in raw solvent aggression you get back in repeatability and in the lines you stopped paying: no hazardous waste manifest, no vapour survey, no fire cabinet, no operator in an open bath. The wash chemistry recirculates through a three-stage filter instead of going to waste, so your consumable becomes five 20-micron cores every few weeks rather than a drum of solvent every few days.

Run your own four-line model this month — solvent, people, compliance, bath carry-over — and put the number next to the quotation you are about to request. Factories that do this stop debating solvent on principle and decide it on arithmetic.

Next step: send us your flux type and a photo of a caked pallet. We will tell you which water-based agent matches your soil and what the cycle looks like — and if solvent genuinely is the only answer for your chemistry, we will say so.

ARTICLE 03720 degrees: why a rotating basket beats a spray tunnel for fixtures

Fixtures are three-dimensional and full of shadows. What rotation plus offset spray rods does that a flat curtain cannot — and where blind zones hide.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2020 user manual and the Southern Machinery technical documents.

A spray tunnel cleans boards because boards are flat. Fixtures are not flat. A wave soldering pallet is a three-dimensional object with mask windows, pockets, threads, spring channels and hold-down pins — and every one of those features casts a shadow that a flat spray curtain cannot reach.

This is why fixture cleaning fails in tunnels and succeeds in baskets. The SME-5200 puts the load in a round SUS304 basket, up to a metre across and two hundred millimetres high, and turns it. While the basket rotates, three liquid spray rods and three water spray rods — above, below and at the front side — lay their curtains across the moving load. Rotation means every face of every fixture passes through every curtain; offset nozzles mean the curtains overlap instead of leaving seams. The manual calls the result even spray pressure with no blind cleaning area, and that phrase is doing enormous work.

Think about the geometry honestly. In a tunnel, the underside of a mask window faces down and sees whatever the lower bars throw at it, once, in a straight line. In a rotating basket, that same underside spends part of every revolution facing up, sideways and down — it cannot hide. Springs and pins that shadow each other in a static load take turns being exposed as the basket turns.

The second half of the method is pressure you can read. Cleaning and rinse pressure gauges sit on the panel beside electrical pressure sensors, and the machine alarms if pressure falls below 2.0 or climbs above 7.0 kg/cm². Too low and the curtain is a drizzle that wets the flux instead of stripping it; too high and you are blasting seals and driving liquid where it should not go. A number on a gauge turns spray quality from a feeling into a setpoint.

Where blind zones hide in practice: nested fixtures stacked flat against each other, small pallets lying face to face, and baskets loaded so full that the load becomes a solid block. The fix is loading discipline and basket inserts that keep parts separated — which is why we ask what your fixtures actually look like before we quote a basket arrangement.

Send us a photo of how your pallets currently stack in a basket or on a trolley. We will tell you the loading pattern and the insert arrangement that keeps every face exposed — or tell you honestly if your fixture geometry needs a different machine.

ARTICLE 04Three-stage filtration is where the running cost actually lives

2 mm, 100 µm, 20 µm: what each stage catches, why chemistry life is measured in weeks, and the filter-change rhythm that keeps cost predictable.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2020 user manual and the Southern Machinery technical documents.

Ask what a cleaning machine costs to run and most answers are a shrug and a drum of chemistry. The real answer is in the filter stack, and the SME-5200 makes it unusually legible: three stages, each with one job.

Stage one is a 2 mm stainless screen sitting where it protects the pump. Its job is not cleanliness, it is survival — solder balls, labels, wire offcuts and chunk debris stop here instead of in the pump impeller. Stage two is a 100 µm stainless screen that catches the solids small enough to pass stage one but large enough to be re-sprayed onto your fixtures as new contamination. Stage three is five 20 µm filter cores, standard 20-inch elements, that pull the fine flux and suspended residue out and return genuinely clean liquid to the tank.

Why three instead of one fine filter? Because a 20 µm core loaded with solder balls blocks in days and costs you both filtration and uptime. Coarse stages are cheap insurance for the expensive stage. The manual quotes 20 µm as the machine's filtration accuracy, and that number is only achievable because the two screens ahead of it do the rough work.

The consequence for running cost is the point of this article. In a single-pass system, chemistry is used once and dumped: you buy a tank of liquid, run it until it is too dirty, and pay again to dispose of it. In the SME-5200's closed loop, liquid is recirculated, filtered and reused continuously, and a compressed-air blow-back at the end of the wash recovers the liquid left in pipes, rods and fixtures back into the tank. Your chemistry consumption stops being proportional to cycles and starts being proportional to what actually leaves on the fixtures — which is very little.

So the consumable rhythm becomes predictable: five 20 µm cores per set, changed every 15 to 30 days depending on soil load, swapped in three moves — release pressure, undo six screws on the barrel, change the cores. That is the entire recurring cost story, and it fits on one line of a maintenance plan.

Check your current system this week: can you name its filtration stages and its chemistry change interval? If the answer is a shrug, that shrug is a cost line. Send us your cycle count per week and we will model your core change interval and chemistry consumption honestly.

ARTICLE 05Water-based is not a compromise — it is the design

The manual forbids solvent on this machine for a reason. What water-based chemistry can and cannot dissolve, and how temperature and time close the gap.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2020 user manual and the Southern Machinery technical documents.

There is a romantic idea that solvent cleans better because it cleans faster. It is romantic because it ignores what faster costs and what water-based chemistry can actually do when you give it the three things it needs: heat, time and mechanics.

Start with the rule, because it is absolute on this machine. The SME-5200 user manual forbids volatile organic cleaning solvents outright — fire and explosion risk — so the question is not whether water-based can match solvent, it is how water-based is engineered to do the job at all. The answer is in three parameters you control on the panel.

Heat: the wash liquid is heated from room temperature up to 80 °C, normally set at 40–45 °C. Flux residue is a temperature problem as much as a chemistry problem; rosin and baked activator soften and dissolve in hot water-based agent in a way they simply do not in cold. Time: the wash runs five to fifteen minutes, chosen per soil level, which is an order of magnitude longer than a solvent dip and precisely why it can be gentler and still win. Mechanics: the rotating basket and the 720-degree spray curtain deliver the agitation that solvent soaking gets from nothing at all.

What water-based cannot do is dissolve cured conformal coating or truly carbonised residue in one cycle — and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling you a second cycle. The honest position is that heavy baked soil gets the long end of the range: fifteen minutes, hotter liquid, and sometimes a second pass. The trials on production pallets at a Schneider Electric factory included heavily contaminated fixtures, and the before/after photographs in the validation report are the argument, not this paragraph.

The trade, stated plainly: solvent is faster per dip and worse at everything else — fire load, vapour, waste, bath carry-over, and an operator standing in it. Water-based is slower per cycle and better at everything else, including the one thing that matters most on a production floor: the tenth fixture is as clean as the first, because the bath is filtered, not fouled.

If you are unsure which side of the line your soil sits on, do not guess from a datasheet. Send a caked pallet for a trial cycle and read the before/after photographs yourself — that is the only test that transfers to your line.

ARTICLE 06Batch cleaning is a process step — schedule it like one

Recipes, saved cycles, password-protected setpoints and a predictable basket rate. The difference between cleaning fixtures and running a fixture-cleaning process.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2020 user manual and the Southern Machinery technical documents.

There is a difference between cleaning fixtures and running a fixture-cleaning process, and the difference shows up in your third month, not your first week. Cleaning fixtures is an activity. A process is the evidence that the activity happened the same way, on the same load, at the same temperature, every time.

Every factory already has the model for this: reflow. Nobody runs an oven without a profile and a record. Yet fixture cleaning — which protects the same joints from the same contamination — usually runs on habit: someone soaks, someone scrubs, someone decides it looks clean enough.

The method is four habits, and the SME-5200 was built around them. One: a recipe per fixture type — wash, rinse and dry times plus the three temperatures, saved on the Mitsubishi PLC touch panel and recalled by name, not re-dialled by hand each load. Two: live monitoring where it matters — PID temperature control on liquid, water and air heaters, pressure gauges backed by electrical sensors, tank level switches that stop heaters before they dry-fire. Three: faults that name themselves — pressure out of band, heater over-temperature at +10 °C tolerance, low level, door opened mid-cycle — each stops the machine and says what tripped. Four: settings that cannot drift — soft parameters are password-protected, so the cycle quality signed off is the cycle the machine runs on night shift.

Once fixture cleaning is a process, it compounds. The recipe library makes a new fixture type a ten-minute qualification instead of a week of experiments. The alarm history turns maintenance from calendar-driven to condition-driven — you change cores when pressure tells you, not when the month turns. And when a customer asks how you control fixture cleanliness, the answer is a recipe list and an alarm log, not a promise.

The operational payoff is the pallet queue disappearing. A predictable cycle means fixture cleaning becomes a scheduled load between shifts instead of an interruption during them; the wave solder machine stops waiting for a clean carrier.

If your fixture cleaning has no recipe, no monitor and no record yet, start with the free audit: send your fixture mix and pallet count per shift, and we will show you what the process version of your current bench looks like — including what it costs today.

ARTICLE 07What a fixture cleaner changes about your line

Pallet queues, solvent cabinets, bench variance and the argument between production and quality. The operational side-effects nobody puts in a brochure.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2020 user manual and the Southern Machinery technical documents.

Brochures talk about cleanliness. Nobody talks about what the floor looks like after the scrubbing bench and the solvent bath are gone — and the floor is where the savings actually land.

The first change is the pallet queue. Hand cleaning is a batch operation hidden inside a flow line: pallets pile up, wait for an operator, get scrubbed one at a time, and wait again on the clean side. Every pallet in that queue is a board not being held, and every handling is a mask window knocked and a pin bent. A batch machine with a saved recipe turns the queue into a schedule: load at the end of the shift, unload at the start, and the wave solder line draws from a known-clean stock.

The second change is the chemistry shelf. Solvent drums, the fire cabinet, the vapour survey, the hazardous-waste manifest, the gloves and the ventilation — an entire compliance inventory that exists only because cleaning was manual and flammable. Water-based batch cleaning replaces the shelf with two 80-litre tanks, a dosing rhythm and a filter barrel, and the waste question shrinks to a drain connection and a box of spent cores.

The third change is the argument between production and quality. On a bench line, quality wants longer soaking and production wants pallets back now, and the operator in the middle absorbs both. On a recipe-driven machine the argument becomes a setpoint: the cycle is saved, the temperature is held by PID, the pressure is monitored, and the conversation moves to what the data says. This is the quiet win every plant manager notices around month three.

The fourth change is people and noise. Nobody planned a career around scrubbing pallets in solvent vapour; the operators the machine frees move to inspection and kitting. And because the cabinet is lined with sound-proof cotton and holds at or below 70 dB, the machine can sit beside the line instead of in a shed at the far end of the yard — which is itself a logistics saving nobody puts in the brochure.

None of this is on a spec sheet, which is exactly why it should be walked on your floor before you believe one. Ask us for a configuration against your actual layout — the queue maths, the shelf inventory and the staffing shift — and see what your line looks like when fixture cleaning stops being a place.

ARTICLE 08Before you buy a fixture cleaner, run these numbers

A four-line payback method with your own labour cost, your own basket rate, your own price — plus the yield savings that make the real number better.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2020 user manual and the Southern Machinery technical documents.

Most payback conversations about cleaning machines are dishonest in the same direction: the vendor's spreadsheet finds savings you will never collect. Here is the opposite method — four lines, your numbers, and a bias toward under-claiming.

Line one: what does the bench cost today? Count the operators who scrub or soak fixtures, their loaded wage, their hours. That recurring number is what the machine is bought against. Line two: what does the machine free? Be honest — a batch cleaner removes the repeatable scrubbing hours, not every handling hour. Use the operators it actually replaces. Line three: the price you were actually quoted, not a list price. Line four: divide — months equal price over annual freed labour divided by twelve. Under twelve months and it is a financial decision, not a capital debate.

Then run the same arithmetic against throughput, because a cleaner that cannot keep up with your pallet loop is a queue with a heater in it. The batch maths is addition, not division: wash plus rinse plus dry. At the manual's mid-range — ten minutes wash, two rinse, fifteen dry — a cycle is about twenty-seven minutes, roughly seventeen baskets in an eight-hour shift before your load and unload allowance. Multiply by fixtures per basket and compare against your pallets per shift, not your best day.

Now the two savings this method deliberately leaves out, because they are yours to prove: the yield you stop losing — mask windows that seal again, solder balls that stop transferring, ICT and coating failures that trace back to fixtures — and the compliance stack you stop paying, the solvent drums, the waste manifests and the vapour surveys. Every factory that starts measuring fixture-related defects finds they were hiding in the soldering cost line.

The calculator on this page runs lines one through four with your inputs and nothing pre-baked, so you can put it in front of your CFO without a salesperson in the room.

Then send us the four numbers plus a photo of your dirtiest pallet. We will turn them into a configuration sheet — basket envelope, cycle times, chemistry, installation checklist — and a quotation that matches the arithmetic you already trust.

13 — FAQ

Answers to the questions this machine raises

What does the SME-5200 actually clean?
Wave soldering pallets and carriers, reflow oven coolers, selective-soldering fixtures, SMT pallets and trays — anything that fits the φ1000 × 200 mm basket envelope up to 450 mm cleaning height. The residue it removes is baked-on flux, solder balls, grease and dust from the soldering process.
Can I use solvent to clean faster?
No — and this is a design position, not a preference. The user manual states that volatile organic cleaning solvents are strictly forbidden on this machine because they may cause fire or explosion. The SME-5200 is engineered for water-based cleaning agents; heat, time, rotation and pressure do the work solvent would, without the fire load, VOC exposure or hazardous-waste manifest.
How long is one cycle, and what is the throughput?
Wash 5–15 minutes, rinse 1–2 minutes, dry 10–20 minutes, plus about a minute of liquid flow-back — all set on the panel per soil level. A typical mid-soil cycle is around 25–35 minutes, so roughly 14–19 baskets in an 8-hour shift before your load and unload allowance. Count fixtures per basket to get your real pallet rate.
What water and chemistry does it need?
Tap water for the 80 L rinse tank — no DI plant required for fixture rinsing — and a water-based cleaning agent for the 80 L wash tank, selected for your flux type. The closed-loop three-stage filtration keeps the wash chemistry alive for weeks; your main consumable is the set of five 20 µm cores, typically changed every 15–30 days.
How much floor space and what utilities?
The machine footprint is about 1.4 × 2.0 m (L 1400 × W 2000 × H 1500 mm) with 1.5 m clear in front and 1 m at the side for service. Utilities: AC 380 V 50 Hz 63 A (about 33 kW), compressed air 0.5–0.7 MPa at 400–600 L/min, a tap-water feed, drains for spent liquid and rinse water, and one Φ120 mm vent to outside extraction.
Will it damage delicate fixtures or loose parts?
The load rotates in the basket rather than being blasted on a conveyor, and spray pressure is held even across the rods with no blind zone. Springs, hold-down pins and small components stay in place with the right basket inserts — the Schneider trials included hold-down components with springs and pins cleaned without disassembly.
What protects the machine and the operator?
Pressure alarms below 2.0 and above 7.0 kg/cm², heater over-temperature protection at +10 °C tolerance, tank level switches against dry running and overflow, and a door guard switch that stops the cycle if the cover opens mid-run. Diaphragm pumps handle liquid fill and drain so nobody lifts or spills hot chemistry.
How do I get a quotation?
Send photos and dimensions of your dirtiest fixtures, your flux type, pallet count per shift and your floor plan to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. You get a configuration sheet with basket envelope, cycle times and chemistry sized to your product — usually within one working day, with a cleaning trial on your own pallets before you commit.
